phases.name: Define
phases.question: What must it do, for whom, in which markets?

phases.name: Concept
phases.question: Does a design exist that meets the intent under the process rules?

phases.name: EVT
phases.question: Does the design work? Hand-built or soft-tooled units.

phases.name: DVT
phases.question: Does it meet every requirement and pass certification, built on production tooling?

phases.name: PVT
phases.question: Can the factory build it at rate and yield?

phases.name: Mass production
phases.question: Is it being built, shipped and supported?

phases.name: In service / end of life
phases.question: Is it working in the field, repairable and recoverable at end of life?

effort_notes: Compliance and DFM start on day one. If you don't know the creepage distances or the moulding draft angle at concept stage, you redesign the PCB or enclosure at DVT, after tooling money is spent.

Mechanical, electronics and firmware run side by side, linked by interfaces (board outline and mounting holes, connector positions, heat load, pinout). Freeze those interfaces early so the teams can work in parallel.
Simulation is front-loaded, before prototypes exist. Physical test is back-loaded, to confirm what simulation predicted.
overlap_drivers: Concurrent engineering maximises overlap: shared CAD and part libraries, early supplier involvement, cross-discipline design reviews.
Long-lead items pull decisions forward: injection-mould tooling takes 6 to 10 weeks and certification test slots are booked months ahead.
Software never really stops: with over-the-air updates, firmware keeps changing after launch.

meeting_point: Every discipline's primitives meet at interfaces. A PCB's mounting holes are a mechanical interface, its heat output a thermal interface, its connector pinout an electrical interface, and the firmware's fault state a user interface. Most product failures happen at those boundaries rather than inside one discipline.
